## Welcome to Orlando

Michael noted that this was Orlando's first status meeting, late in the day for him, and suggested starting with introductions.

Orlando ([@0rlych1kk4](https://github.com/0rlych1kk4), "Orly" for short) is based in the Philippines. His background is in systems engineering, information security architecture and Rust development, with a focus on secure software and cryptographic integration. His first contribution to OQS was the QR-UOV integration in liboqs ([PR #2582](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2582)), and he is continuing with follow-up work on consolidating the AES back-end and synchronizing with upstream. Rodrigo thanked Orlando for his two main contributions. The second is liboqs-rust: Orlando has said he is willing to look after it in the same way that Douglas does for liboqs-python. This would move liboqs-rust out of caretaker status, with one committer actively maintaining it. Rodrigo introduced the other attendees and explained the meeting format: status meetings every Tuesday, alternating between 10:00 and 12:30 US Eastern, and a TSC meeting about every five weeks that is less technical and more about running the project. Orlando is welcome to attend regularly.

Douglas welcomed Orlando. He said that, especially for liboqs-rust, Orlando should ask or tag people whenever he needs feedback or responses to keep things moving. Michael thanked Orlando for his work so far and asked to be tagged on GitHub for anything that needs his attention, since untagged activity may slip past him.

Hart has been discussing this with Douglas and Rodrigo by email and looking at what other LF projects do. He asked how people feel about GitHub Copilot. Rodrigo said his own experience with Copilot for coding had not been great compared with Claude and ChatGPT, though it was good for other, more Microsoft-related tasks. He had not used it much, and it was about nine months ago, so he could not say which models he had used. Douglas noted that Copilot now appears to offer models such as Claude Opus. Hart said Copilot may be the easiest option. It integrates well with the GitHub setup OQS already uses, and it may be possible to get it through LF IT at a large LF-wide discount, which would likely be more cost-effective than other options. This still has to be negotiated with LF IT and will probably take a couple of weeks to firm up. Hart will be at a conference in India next week, which will slow things down.

It would be good for OQS work to be resourced from within OQS.

Hart asked whether people would be comfortable with Copilot if they did not have to use Microsoft's own models. Douglas will look into what is available and possibly try it out.

## liboqs

### 0.17 planning

Douglas set up a prioritized backlog project board, and Rodrigo has done an initial prioritization for 0.17 based on the backlog, open PRs and recent discussions. He found the board very helpful. It reflects the timeline from last week's TSC meeting: all remaining round 3 algorithms (FAEST, SQIsign and SDitH) should be merged into liboqs by the next TSC meeting on November 24. To allow two weeks for review, PRs should be ready for review by November 10. GitHub project boards do not directly support such dates, so Rodrigo has worked around this to show them.

The items marked essential for 0.17 are the round 3 algorithms and disabling Classic McEliece by default ([PR #2640](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/liboqs/pull/2640)), which should be a very straightforward PR. Other issues are grouped as "desired" or "addition"; everyone is welcome to add, change or drop items. Which of these make the cut will depend on the time available before release. No one objected to the essential items.

## OQS-OpenSSL 3 provider

**Code point assignment ([PR #852](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/852)).** After QR-UOV was merged in liboqs, Rodrigo opened a corresponding provider PR ([PR #849](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/849)). Michael pointed out that, with the provider's current approach, there would not be enough code points for all the signature variants, because the provider assigns a code point to every algorithm whether or not it is enabled for TLS. Rodrigo therefore split the work into two PRs. The first, PR #852, is a major refactor of code point assignment for both signatures and KEMs, so that code points are only assigned where needed, leaving plenty of room for new algorithms. Its main consequence is that it definitively drops the ability to build the provider against older liboqs versions. That was already broken in practice by changes in liboqs 0.14 and 0.15, and the stated policy is that the latest provider goes with the latest liboqs. Even so, Rodrigo asked everyone to look at the PR and confirm they are comfortable with this. Once it is resolved, QR-UOV and the remaining round 3 signature algorithms will follow.

Michael asked whether the BIKE-L1 TLS question ([issue #850](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/850)) is addressed in this PR. BIKE-L1 and its hybrids had been left disabled for TLS so that testing covered an algorithm supported by the provider but not in TLS; Michael had argued on the PR that this surprises external users and downstream projects. Rodrigo said he had changed this that morning, and PR #852 now re-enables BIKE-L1 for TLS.

**Other activity.** A PR adding advisory code-complexity CI ([PR #845](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/845)) has been merged. The open issue and PR on splitting out hybrid support ([issue #847](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/issues/847), [PR #855](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/855)) are a larger discussion of their own. Rodrigo has also created a project board for the provider, mirroring the liboqs one. Douglas noted that it is currently private (visible only within the OQS organization). Rodrigo wants it public, and Douglas will look at how to change that.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (all):** Review [PR #852](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider/pull/852), in particular the end of support for building against older liboqs versions.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Douglas):** Make the oqs-provider project board public. (Note after the meeting: Douglas doesn't have permission to do this, so Michael or Rodrigo will need to do it.)

## Language wrappers and release timing

Rodrigo noted that, as part of the caretaker work ([PR #333](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/pull/333)), he has documented the governance status of each repository. Once the caretaker language lands, several repositories will be labelled as under caretaker status or unsupported.

Michael suggested that, before anything is put in writing, the maintainers of the supported wrappers (now including Orlando, and Douglas for liboqs-python) agree to release soon after the next liboqs release, as has been agreed for liboqs and oqs-provider. Rodrigo said that a provider timeline has not actually been agreed yet. The agreement is for all round 3 algorithms to be in liboqs by the next TSC meeting, with the provider PRs following within a day of each one landing. If the code point refactor goes to plan, he can commit to a provider release about a week after liboqs. Douglas said liboqs-python has no algorithm-specific code, so new algorithms need no work. It just needs any open issues and PRs dealt with, testing, and a version bump. Rodrigo suggested two to three weeks after liboqs for the wrappers, so that everything is released before mid-December, which is effectively the end of the year for many people.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Release oqs-provider about one week after the liboqs 0.17 release.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (maintainers of supported wrappers):** Release within two to three weeks of the liboqs 0.17 release, before mid-December.
